client: I've been having a really hard time at work lately, and honestly I wasn't sure if coming here would even do anything. There's this colleague, Jessica, who keeps presenting my ideas in meetings like they're her own, and my manager doesn't seem to notice at all. It's making me feel completely invisible, and I keep worrying that if she keeps doing this, people will start thinking I'm not contributing anything and my job could be at risk.
therapist: What you're describing sounds genuinely painful — having your contributions go unrecognized, and then carrying the weight of worrying about what that means for your future, is a lot to hold. I'm glad you came today, even with that uncertainty about whether it would help. I'd love to understand more about what "invisible" feels like for you in those moments — is it more about the frustration of being overlooked, or does it tap into something deeper about how you see your value at work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Honestly, it's both, but I think the deeper thing is that it makes me question whether I actually matter there at all. Like, if my ideas can just be taken and no one even notices, maybe I'm just... replaceable. And that thought terrifies me, because work is one of the few places I felt like I was actually good at something.
therapist: That fear of being replaceable — especially in a space where you've built a real sense of competence and worth — that's such a significant thing to sit with. It sounds like work hasn't just been a job for you, but almost a foundation for believing in yourself. I'm curious, when you say it's "one of the few places" you felt good at something, what does that tell you about how you've been seeing yourself in other areas of your life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess it tells me that I don't feel particularly good at much else right now. Outside of work I feel kind of... adrift, like I don't have strong friendships or hobbies that make me feel capable or valued. So if this one thing gets taken away, or if people stop seeing my contributions, I'm not sure what's left to hold onto.
therapist: What you're describing — that feeling of having so little to anchor yourself to beyond work — sounds really lonely, and it makes sense that this situation with Jessica feels so threatening. It's like work has been quietly carrying a weight it was never meant to carry alone. I want to gently explore that with you — when did you start to feel that drift outside of work, and do you have a sense of what might have contributed to those connections or interests fading?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's been gradual, maybe over the last two or three years. I moved to a new city for this job, and I told myself I'd build a social life once I got settled, but somehow that never really happened and I just kept pouring more of myself into work instead. And now it feels like such a long time has passed that I wouldn't even know where to start with building connections again.
therapist: That pattern of "I'll get to it once I'm settled" is so understandable, and yet it has a quiet way of stretching into years before we realize it. What strikes me is that even as you're describing something that sounds quite heavy — this long period of isolation — there's a kind of matter-of-fact quality to how you're telling it, almost like you've made a kind of peace with it, or perhaps just gotten used to it. I wonder, underneath that, how does it actually feel to look back on those two or three years?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I actually stop and think about it instead of just pushing through... it feels like a waste. Like I watched time pass and kept telling myself it was temporary, but it wasn't, and now I feel this guilt about it, like I should have tried harder. I think the matter-of-fact thing is just how I've learned to talk about it so I don't have to fully feel how sad it actually is.
therapist: The fact that you can name that — that the calm way of speaking is actually a kind of protection — takes real self-awareness, and it matters that you let yourself feel some of that sadness just now. That guilt you're carrying, the sense that you "should have tried harder," is worth looking at gently, because I wonder if it's really fair to the version of you who was just trying to survive a big transition and find their footing. What do you think you needed back then that you didn't quite give yourself permission to reach for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I needed to let myself admit that I was struggling instead of just performing like everything was fine. I kept telling myself that asking for help or reaching out to people would make me seem weak or needy, so I just... didn't. And I'm not sure I even know how to stop doing that now, because it's become such a reflex.
therapist: What you just named is really significant — that hiding struggle became so automatic it no longer feels like a choice, just how you move through the world. And yet here you are, in this room, actually saying it out loud, which is itself a quiet act of doing the very thing you've been afraid to do. I'm curious — as you hear yourself say that now, does it actually feel as dangerous as that old reflex has always warned you it would?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: In this moment, no, it doesn't feel as dangerous as I expected, which is a little disorienting to be honest. But I think that's partly because this feels like a contained, safe space, and I'm not sure that translates to real life where the stakes feel so much higher. Like, saying this to you is one thing, but the idea of actually showing vulnerability to a colleague or someone I might want to be friends with still feels really exposing and risky.
therapist: It's really honest of you to name that distinction — that safety here doesn't automatically translate out there, and that's not you being pessimistic, that's you being realistic about how vulnerability works. The stakes do feel different with people whose opinions of us are less certain. I'm wondering though, what specifically do you imagine happening if someone in your real life saw you struggle — what's the story you tell yourself about how they'd respond?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the story I tell myself is that they'd see me as a burden, or that they'd pull away because nobody really wants to deal with someone else's problems when they have their own. There's also this fear that if I show weakness to someone like a potential friend, they'll decide early on that I'm too much and just not bother. It's like I've already decided how it ends before it even begins, which I can see is probably not helping me.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — that you're essentially writing the rejection before the other person has even had a chance to respond, which means the fear is doing the work of protecting you before any real risk even exists. That's a very human thing to do, but it also means you've been carrying the pain of rejection without ever actually getting the connection that might have come instead. I'd love to explore with you — where do you think that story first came from, because beliefs this strong usually have a history?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it probably goes back to when I was younger and I did try to open up to people and it didn't go well. There was a period in school where I went through something difficult and the friends I thought I had kind of drifted away instead of showing up, and I think I just internalized that as proof that being a burden drives people away. It's strange to connect that to what's happening now with work and Jessica, but I can see how that same belief is running underneath all of it.
therapist: What you just connected is profound — that a younger version of you learned a very painful lesson from people who weren't able to show up, and you've been carrying that as a truth about yourself ever since, rather than as a truth about those particular people in that particular moment. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, like there's a lot moving through you as you make these connections, and I want to make sure we don't rush past how significant this is. That child who reached out and was met with silence deserved so much better — and I'm wondering, does part of you still believe that what happened then was somehow your fault?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think part of me does still believe that, even though logically I know kids drift apart and people are just bad at handling hard things. But there's this stubborn little voice that says if I had been more likeable, or less intense, or just easier to be around, they would have stayed. I've never really said that out loud before and it feels uncomfortable sitting here with it now.
therapist: The fact that you've never said that out loud before, and you're saying it now, is really courageous — and I want to honour how much it costs to sit with something that tender. That voice telling you that you were "too much" is one of the cruellest things we can carry, because it turns a story about other people's limitations into a story about your own unworthiness. I want to gently offer this back to you: what would you say to a child you cared about who believed that people left because they weren't likeable enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
